title: Origin is scheme, host, and port.
lede: Same-origin policy: two pages share origin iff scheme, host, and port match. https://app.com ≠ http://app.com ≠ https://app.com:4443 ≠ https://api.app.com. Cookies use site (eTLD+1, plate 233), which is coarser. CORS (plate 15) is the browser asking the other origin for permission.
diagram: Left: https://a.com/x and https://a.com/y — same. Right: https://a.com vs https://api.a.com — different origin, maybe same-site. Caption: file:// origins are opaque. null origin from sandboxed iframes.
what: The browser’s isolation unit for DOM, storage, and (mostly) cookies’ cousin rules.
why: XSS is same-origin execution (plate 234). Fetch to another origin is CORS.
trap: Thinking subdomains share origin. document.domain hacks. Comparing origin to hostname only.

title: CSP lists who may run script.
lede: Content-Security-Policy is a response header. script-src 'self' https://cdn.example 'nonce-abc': inline script without that nonce does not run, even if XSS injected it (plate 234). default-src, img-src, connect-src, frame-ancestors. Report-Only to measure first.
diagram: 1 CSP: script-src 'nonce-R4nd'. 2 <script nonce=R4nd src=/app.js>. 3 injected <script>alert(1)</script> blocked. Caption: 'unsafe-inline' disables the win. Hashes for static inline.
what: An allowlist the browser enforces. Defense in depth, not a sanitizer replacement.
why: XSS residual. Clickjacking (frame-ancestors). Data exfil via connect-src.
trap: unsafe-inline and unsafe-eval in production. Nonce that is static. CSP only on the homepage.

title: bcrypt cost 12 is 2^12 iterations.
lede: Password hashes must be slow (plate 31). bcrypt cost N ≈ 2^N Blowfish setups. 12 is ~200–400 ms on a 2020s CPU; 13 is ~2×. argon2id is the current winner (memory-hard). Store algorithm+cost+salt+hash in one string. Verify is compare the digest, not == on the password.
diagram: facts: cost 10 ~50 ms; 12 ~300 ms; 14 ~1 s; salt ≥16 B; never MD5/SHA1. Caption: work factor should grow with hardware. Timing-safe compare (plate 359).
what: Adaptive KDF. Cost is a parameter you store and can raise on next login.
why: Offline dump resistance. 1e9 MD5/s vs 3 bcrypt/s/core.
trap: cost 4 in prod. Truncating bcrypt at 72 bytes silently. HMAC-SHA256 as a password hash without a KDF.

title: JWT is header.payload.signature.
lede: Three base64url segments. Header: alg, typ. Payload: claims (sub, exp, iat, iss, aud) — readable by anyone. Signature: HMAC or RSA over header.payload. Verify alg, iss, aud, exp. The payload is not encrypted (that’s JWE).
diagram: 1 split 3. 2 check alg against an allowlist (never none). 3 verify sig with the right key. 4 exp < now → 401. Caption: HS256 needs a secret; RS256 verifies with the issuer’s public key (JWKS).
what: A signed set of claims. Stateless if you don’t revoke; revocation needs a denylist or short exp + refresh.
why: OAuth access tokens, session substitutes. Interviews: why you still need TLS and why alg=none was a CVE.
trap: Trusting payload before sig. Accepting alg from the header blindly. Storing PII in JWT and logging it (plate 271). 10-year exp.

title: A prepared statement parses once. $1 is data.
lede: SQL injection (plate 16) is the parser seeing user bytes as syntax. Prepared/parameterized: parse SELECT … WHERE id=$1 once; bind a typed value. The value cannot close the quote because it never enters the parser as text. ORMs that interpolate strings are not prepared.
diagram: Left: '… WHERE name=\''+user+'\'' → OR 1=1. Right: PQexecParams($1, varchar). facts: PREPARE/EXECUTE; psycopg2 extras; JDBC ?. Caption: IDENTIFIERS (table names) cannot be bound — allowlist those.
what: Protocol-level bind. Types on the wire. Plan reuse is a bonus.
why: The actual fix, not ‘escape quotes’.
trap: format(‘… %s …’, user) in Python. Prisma/Knex raw. Binding a whole IN () list by concatenating anyway.

title: ../ is not a filename.
lede: open(userPath) with userPath = ../../etc/passwd walks out of the uploads dir. Fix: resolve to canonical (realpath), then check prefix of the allowed root with a boundary (root + sep). Reject NUL bytes, backslashes on Windows, encoded %2e%2e.
diagram: Left: /var/app/uploads/ + ../../../etc/passwd. Right: realpath, startsWith(/var/app/uploads/). Caption: zip slip is the same bug inside archives.
what: Untrusted path segments vs a rooted tree. Canonicalize then prefix-check.
why: File download/upload endpoints. Static file servers.
trap: startswith without the trailing slash (/var/app/uploads vs /var/app/uploads_evil). Decoding after the check.

title: SSRF is your server fetching their URL.
lede: The app does GET(userUrl) and returns the body. Attacker passes http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/ (cloud credentials) or http://127.0.0.1:6379/. You are a proxy into the VPC. Allowlist schemes+hosts; block link-local, loopback, RFC1918; do not follow redirects off-allowlist.
diagram: Left: webhook URL from user, no check. Right: allow https://hooks.slack.com/… only; resolve DNS and re-check IPs (DNS rebinding). Caption: file:// and gopher:// in old parsers.
what: Confused deputy (plate 361) on the network. The server’s trust is the bug.
why: Cloud metadata, internal admin ports, Redis unauth.
trap: Blacklisting 127.0.0.1 but not 2130706433 or [::1] or 169.254.169.254. Following 302 to an internal IP.

title: memcmp returns early. Secrets must not.
lede: memcmp / == on bytes stops at the first difference: attacker times the response to learn the secret prefix. Use a constant-time compare (CRYPTO_memcmp, hmac.compare_digest, crypto.timingSafeEqual). Apply to tokens, CSRF, webhook signatures — not to ‘admin’ vs ‘user’ usernames (those need other controls).
diagram: Left: if (token[i]!=got[i]) return 401 — 50 µs vs 200 µs. Right: xor all bytes, OR into acc, compare acc to 0. Caption: network jitter hides small leaks; still do it. Don’t early-return on length either without care.
what: Data-independent time for equal-length secret compares. Lengths should be public or padded.
why: API keys, reset tokens, HMAC headers.
trap: hash_equals then a second ==. Comparing hashes with != in a high-resolution local attack. SHA256(password) without a KDF (plate 354).

title: HSTS remembers HTTPS. The first HTTP visit is still open.
accent: The first HTTP visit is still open.
lede: Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains; preload. After one HTTPS response, the browser will not speak HTTP to that host for max-age. Preload list bakes it into Chrome. The first visit (or a captive portal) can still be MITM without preload.
diagram: 1 first GET http://bank — MITM possible. 2 HTTPS + HSTS. 3 later http upgraded internally, never sent. Caption: max-age=0 disables. Mixed content is a separate browser rule.
what: A browser pin to TLS. Server-side HTTPS-only is not the same as HSTS.
why: SSL stripping. Why preload exists for banks.
trap: HSTS on a host that still has HTTP-only subdomains. Tiny max-age. HTTP→HTTPS redirect without HSTS (the redirect itself is strippable).

title: The confused deputy has your power, their intent.
lead: The confused deputy has your power,
lede: A deputy (your browser, your server, your LLM) is allowed to do X. An attacker aims it at Y. CSRF (plate 30): browser sends cookies to your POST. SSRF (plate 358): server fetches internal. Prompt injection (plate 46): model calls a tool. Same pattern: ambient authority + untrusted input.
diagram: Box1 CSRF cookie ambient. Box2 SSRF URL ambient. Box3 tool-calling LLM. Caption: capability tokens / CSRF tokens / allowlists / human confirm cut the ambient part.
what: Confused deputy problem (Norm Hardy). Fix authority, don’t just filter strings.
why: Unifies a lot of ‘security bugs’ in one sentence.
trap: Adding a WAF regex and calling it done. An LLM with a DELETE tool and untrusted mail in context.

title: Two keys live during rotation. One dies after.
lede: Rotate a signing or encryption key: generate new, sign with new, verify with both for a grace window, then drop old. JWT kid header selects the key from JWKS. Dual-read, single-write. Secrets in env/files need the same two-phase deploy.
diagram: 1 JWKS has kid A,B. 2 issue with B. 3 accept A or B for 24h. 4 JWKS only B. Caption: KMS/versioned secrets. Short-lived tokens shrink the window (plate 355).
what: Overlap so in-flight tokens/sessions survive. Then delete.
why: Key leak, employee offboarding, yearly crypto hygiene.
trap: Flip the secret in one deploy — all sessions 401. Never deleting the old key. Logging the key material.

title: The auth code is not the token.
lede: OAuth authorization code flow: browser gets a short-lived code at the redirect. The backend (client secret or PKCE) exchanges code at the token endpoint for access (+ refresh). The SPA should not be a confidential client. Access token stays off URL logs.
diagram: 1 /authorize?client_id&redirect&code_challenge. 2 redirect ?code=. 3 POST /token code+verifier → access_token. Caption: implicit flow is deprecated. OpenID adds id_token.
what: Delegation protocol. Code is a one-time ticket. Bearer token is the key (TLS + storage plate 232).
why: Login with Google/GitHub. Why the secret is on the server.
trap: Putting the access token in the redirect fragment and calling it modern. Skipping PKCE on public clients. Using the id_token as an API key at your backend without validating aud.

title: Git stores blobs, trees, commits. Not diffs.
lede: blob = file bytes (hashed). tree = dir listing of name→hash. commit = parent hash + tree hash + author + message. The object id is a hash of the content (SHA-1 historically, SHA-256 repos exist). A ‘diff’ is computed at show time from two trees. Packfiles delta-compress later for disk.
diagram: 1 blob 8f… README. 2 tree 3a… 100644 README → 8f. 3 commit 9c… parent 1b tree 3a. Caption: git cat-file -p. Content-addressed: same bytes = same hash.
what: A DAG of immutable objects. Branches are names for commits (plate 367).
why: Why rewriting history changes hashes (plate 366). Why empty commit still has an id.
trap: Thinking git stores patch files as the source of truth. Mutating a commit and expecting the hash to stay.

title: The index is the next commit.
lede: Three trees: HEAD (last commit), index/staging (what commit will write), working directory (files). git add copies worktree → index. git commit writes a tree from the index and a commit pointing at HEAD. git reset moves those pointers; the flags decide how far.
diagram: Left: edit file, not add — commit won’t include it. Right: add then edit again — commit has the added bytes, not the last edit. Caption: git status is the three-way diff. restore --staged.
what: A snapshot you build, then name. Not a list of patches.
why: Partial commits, ‘why didn’t my change ship.’
trap: commit -a as a reflex (skips new untracked files, includes everything tracked). Assuming add watches the file.

title: merge adds a node. rebase rewrites hashes.
lede: merge C onto M: if M is ancestor, fast-forward (move the name). Else a new commit with two parents. rebase C onto M: replay C’s unique commits as new objects with new hashes on M. Shared published hashes should not be rebased without coordination.
diagram: Left merge: history shows the join. Right rebase: linear, old C hashes orphaned. Caption: reflog still has them for ~30 days. force-with-lease not force.
what: DAG edit vs DAG append. Conflicts are the same content problem.
why: Branch policy. Why force-push breaks other clones.
trap: rebase of main onto a feature (inverted). rebase after someone pulled your branch. merge --no-ff spam vs always rebase fights.

title: HEAD is a pointer. A branch is a name.
lede: refs/heads/main is a file with a commit hash. HEAD is usually a symbolic ref to that name. Detached HEAD: HEAD is a raw hash — commits you make are reachable only via that hash/reflog until you name them. Tags are names that don’t move (unless -f).
diagram: 1 HEAD → refs/heads/main → 9c3. 2 checkout 9c3^ — detached. 3 branch save — now a name. Caption: git switch -c. origin/main is a remote-tracking name.
what: Names are cheap, movable labels on the object DAG.
why: ‘Where did my commit go?’ Detached. Why deleting a branch doesn’t delete objects immediately.
trap: Committing for an hour detached then checkout main. Thinking origin/main updates without fetch.

title: stdout is data. stderr is diagnostics.
lede: fd 1 stdout: the payload another program should consume. fd 2 stderr: logs, progress, errors — should survive a pipe. cmd | jq sends only stdout to jq. 2>/dev/null hides errors, not data. Exit code (plate 369) is the third channel.
diagram: Left: printf data; fprintf(stderr, log). Right: cmd 2>&1 | tee — merge. Caption: progress bars belong on stderr so | gzip stays valid.
what: Two streams by convention, not by OS law. Both are fds (plate 294).
why: Pipelines, CI logs, why ‘broken pipe’ is SIGPIPE on stdout.
trap: JSON on stderr and errors on stdout. Mixing them then parsing the mix. >/dev/null and wondering where the error went (it’s on 2).

title: 0 succeeded. Nonzero is the error code.
lede: exit(n): 8-bit status. 0 = success for shells and Make. 1 generic; 2 misuse; 127 not found; 128+N killed by signal N (SIGKILL 137). set -e aborts a shell on nonzero. CI is a chain of these integers.
diagram: facts: 0 ok; 1 fail; 127 command not found; 130 SIGINT; 137 OOM/SIGKILL. Caption: waitpid status packing; Python sys.exit.
what: The process’s summary integer. stdout may still have data.
why: Scripts, containers (restartPolicy), Make.
trap: exit(256) which becomes 0. Returning -1 from main. Grep: no match is 1 — ‘failure’ in set -e pipelines.

title: Make is a DAG of files and commands.
lede: target: deps then a recipe. Make compares mtimes: if a dep is newer than the target, run the recipe. Cycles are errors. Parallel -j is safe iff the DAG is the real deps. Phony targets (clean) are names not files.
diagram: app: a.o b.o ; cc -o app a.o b.o. a.o: a.c a.h. Caption: ninja/bazel are the same idea with better graphs. stamp files for ‘always run’.
what: Rebuild = outdated edge. The graph is the API.
why: Compiles, codegen, docker layers conceptually.
trap: Missing a header in deps (stale .o). recipe that doesn’t write the target. Spaces vs tabs.

title: A .so is relocated at load. A .a is copied in.
lede: Static .a: ld copies object code into your binary (plate 325). Shared .so/.dll: load-time or lazy PLT resolve, position-independent code, one text segment shared among processes. ldd, DT_NEEDED, RPATH/RUNPATH vs LD_LIBRARY_PATH.
diagram: Left: huge binary, no runtime dep. Right: libc.so.6 mapped once. Caption: Windows DLL search path is a CVE magnet.
what: When the bytes join your address space. Dynamic needs ABI stability (plate 326).
why: Disk, memory, updates (patch libc without relinking the world).
trap: LD_LIBRARY_PATH in prod as architecture. Mixing two libstdc++.so. Undeclared indirect deps.

title: A container is namespaces plus cgroups, not a VM.
lead: A container is namespaces plus cgroups,
lede: Linux container: PID/mount/net/uts/ipc/user namespaces (clone flags) + cgroups (plate 306) + a rootfs (often overlayfs). Same kernel as the host. A VM has its own kernel and hardware model. Isolation is as good as the kernel + seccomp + dropped caps (plate 304).
diagram: 1 namespaces hide names. 2 cgroups cap resources. 3 overlay: lower image + upper writes. Caption: Docker is UX on runc/containerd. K8s is orchestration.
what: Kernel features composed. Not a hypervisor. /proc/1 in the container is not host init.
why: Density vs isolation. Why a kernel CVE is a container CVE.
trap: --privileged. Mounting docker.sock. Assuming host files are invisible (bind mounts, /proc).

title: strace prints the syscalls. That is the kernel API.
lede: strace -p PID (or strace cmd) uses ptrace to log every syscall: name, args, return, errno, time. That is the process↔kernel interface (plate 287), independent of language. -e trace=file|network to filter. Overhead is real; don’t leave it on in prod.
diagram: Left: openat(AT_FDCWD, "/etc/passwd", O_RDONLY) = 3. Right: connect(5, {sin_port=443}) = 0. Caption: ltrace is libc. dtruss/ktrace on BSD. perf/ebpf for less tax.
what: A trace of traps. Arguments may be truncated pointers.
why: ‘What file is it looking for?’ ‘Which host does it hit?’ First debugging tool on Linux.
trap: Reading errno as success. Following children (-f) on a thread storm. Interpreting a failed open as the one that mattered — later one succeeded.

title: A core dump is the address space at death.
lead: A core dump is the address space
lede: SIGSEGV/SIGABRT with ulimit -c unlimited writes a file of the mm (plus notes: registers, auxv). gdb ./app core; bt. systemd-coredump / apport may intercept. Size ≈ RSS; strip secrets. pip install vs missing debug symbols: you get hex.
diagram: 1 ulimit -c unlimited. 2 crash. 3 gdb bt full. Caption: /proc/sys/kernel/core_pattern. minidump is a subset (Breakpad).
what: A snapshot for postmortem. Not a log. ASLR means addresses differ per run; use symbols.
why: Native crashes, Go panic with GOTRACEBACK=crash.
trap: core_pattern |/dev/null. Shipping without symbols and wondering why bt is empty. Core files in world-readable /tmp with secrets in RAM.

title: #! is the kernel's interpreter line.
lede: execve on a file starting #!/usr/bin/python3 rewrites to execve("/usr/bin/python3", ["python3", script, args]). The kernel does this, not the shell. env: #!/usr/bin/env python3 looks up PATH. chmod +x. CRLF after python3 → interpreter not found.
diagram: Left: ./app.py with shebang. Right: python3 app.py skips shebang as a comment. facts: Linux shebang length cap ~127–256. Caption: env -S for extra args on some systems.
what: A tiny exec protocol. Portable scripts use env; Nix/Guix often pin absolute paths.
why: CLI tools, Docker ENTRYPOINT. Why the script ‘works in python3 x.py’ and ‘not as ./x.py’.
trap: Windows CRLF. Spaces in the interpreter path. Relying on python not python3.
